Random denominators do not automatically bias gradients. For one branch, let G be the summed target gradients, N its target count, and μ=E[G]/E[N]. A second-order expansion gives E[G/N]−μ ≈ [μ Var(N)−Cov(G,N)]/E[N]², componentwise, assuming N>0. Thus numerator–count correlation can cancel denominator-induced bias: if E[G|N]=Nμ, the normalized gradient is exactly unbiased. Random-sample-size means have this property when conditional observations retain the same mean ([Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis](https://web.mit.edu/dimitrib/www/NDP.pdf)). These are statistical deductions applied to the proposed loss.

Fixed 64/64 view counts versus 128 Bernoulli(0.75) terminal assignments give expected view counts 96 terminal/32 reconstruction. Separate 0.5 normalizations preserve equal branch weights; they do not become 0.75/0.25. With one target per view and count-independent conditional gradient means, both schemes have the same expected gradient, apart from empty-branch handling. Bernoulli sampling changes variance through E[1/N]: approximately two-thirds the terminal variance and twice the reconstruction variance versus 64/64, before count-fluctuation corrections. Reconstruction is empty with probability 0.75^128≈10⁻¹⁶.

With multiple masked targets per reconstruction view, even fixed view counts leave target counts random. Correlation between masks-per-view and average target gradients can create finite-sample ratio bias, typically O(1/m) for m independent views; reducing reconstruction views from 64 to about 32 can therefore change expected gradients despite unchanged branch-conditional contexts. Its sign and magnitude require the joint count–gradient distribution. Ratio-estimation research confirms that denominator size and pooling affect finite-sample bias ([Ogliore et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.0797)). Consequently, a variance-only claim requires the conditional-mean assumption.
